entry.dc:title: Changes in earthworm populations following cultivation of undisturbed and former opencast coal-mining land
entry.dc:creator: Scullion J.
entry.dc:description: Earthworm response to a single cultivation sequence was assessed. Cropping and management of cultivated land was similar to that of non-cultivated areas. Effects were measured in a trial on recently replaced opencast mining land. A subsequent survey investigated responses to cultivation on both replaced and undisturbed land at periods since cultivation ranging from 1.5 to 7.5 years. On undisturbed land, adverse effects of cultivation, if any, were short-lived, with numbers of all species, but particularly deep-burrowing species, having recovered or increased after 3 years. However, on replaced land the initial adverse effect appeared to be larger, and recovery from this effect was delayed until at least 5 years after tillage. Different species present (Lumbricus terrestris/ Aporrectodea longa, Lumbricus rubellus/festivus, Aporrectodea caliginosa/Octalasion tyrtaeum and Allolobophora chlorotica) also varied in the extent of the initial reduction and in their rate of recovery. Reasons for different responses to cultivation and implications for the management of replaced land are considered. © 1988.

entry.dc:title: The development of mining and its influence on changes of relief in the Walbrzych Coal Region
entry.dc:creator: Wojcik J.
entry.dc:description: Out of all the components of the natural environment of the Walbrzych Coal Region, relief was the most affected by the development of mining of rock raw materials. Hard coal mining brought about the biggest changes in the relief. The extraction of this raw material resulted in the formation of many mine dumps, settling ponds, and crowded urban and industrial structures near Walbrzych and Boguszow-Gorce. Hard coal mining caused ground settlement which had led to the formation of small hollows in the ground, the so-called subsidence basins. Maximum values of ground settlement amount to over 12 m in that area. Opencast mining of rock raw materials resulted in smaller changes of relief. -from English summary

entry.dc:title: Post glacial history of the Nant Helen opencast site South Wales: implications for land restoration
entry.dc:creator: Chambers F.
entry.prism:publicationName: Occasional Paper University of Keele Department of Geography
entry.dc:description: A proposal to extend opencast mining at Nant Helen Colliery, South Wales, threatened both archaeological sites and a large expanse of upland mire on Mynydd y Drum. Excavations of two cairns and a length of post-medieval trackway were conducted there by the Clwyd-Powys Archaeological Trust in the summer of 1987. These were accompanied by palaeoecological work to ascertain both the post-glacial environmental history of Mynydd y Drum and the contemporary environmental setting of the two cairns. Evidence suggests that the most dramatic impact upon local woodland was in the early Bronze Age. The evidence for former extensive deciduous woodlands on Mynydd y Drum now offers British Coal a wider range of land restoration goals, for consideration when the opencast mining ceases. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: The conservation and amenity value of ball-clay ponds in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, UK
entry.dc:creator: Friday L.E.
entry.dc:description: Opencast mining is the principal method by which ball-clays are extracted from heathland in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, UK. An understanding of the substitute habitats so created is required if the environmental impact of this mode of extraction is to be assessed. This paper investigates the conservation and amenity value of the water bodies arising from 18th and 19th century workings in the Isle of Purbeck. The 16 ball-clay ponds studied varied widely in chemistry and supported a range of freshwater habitats and biotas. Several species of special conservation interest occurred and the ponds had a diverse dragonfly fauna. The acidic heathland ponds represent a habitat of local and diminishing distribution in lowland Britain. The more enriched, circum-neutral ponds supported fish populations of varying quality, some of which may have a considerable amenity value. Collectively, these ponds make a positive contribution to the ecological and landscape diversity of the Isle of Purbeck. © 1988.

entry.dc:title: Earthworms and structure rehabilitation in subsoils and in topsoils affected by opencast mining for coal
entry.dc:creator: Stewart V.I.
entry.dc:description: Because soil structure seems to benefit from the period under grass in a normal rotation, it is widely assumed that grass roots are primarily responsible (Strutt, 1970). Due credit is also given to efficient drainage, adequate inputs of organic matter, lime and microbial activity. However, it is not clear whether the earthworm is a passive exploiter or a causal agent of structure improvement. When the pressures of production end up in severe soil structure deterioration, or when massive soil disturbance and stockpiling ends up in soils restored with little residual structure, experimental evidence suggests that the role of the earthworm is crucial. Evidence will be presented to show how earthworms, in association with all the other factors normally held to be responsible, initiate the development of water-stable, soil granulation. However, evidence will also be presented which shows how certain features of modern agriculture are, to some extent at least, antagonistic to earthworms. In utilizing degraded land, it may be necessary to farm initially for the benefit of the earthworm rather than for yield. This approach must be maintained despite the fact that, in the early stages, it may result in a phase of greater waterlogging and susceptibility to poaching. © 1988 A B Academic Publishers.

entry.dc:title: Thematic mapping of the abandoned mining hazard: A pilot study for the South Wales Coalfield
entry.dc:creator: Statham I.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geological Society Engineering Geology Special Publication
entry.dc:description: The Department of the Environment and the Welsh Office jointly sponsored a South Wales Desk Study into the feasibility of producing thematic maps of the Mining subsidence risk for planners. A method was to be developed and tested for a 25 km<sup>2</sup> Pilot Area centred on Ebbw Vale. The study was started by collecting geological and mining data for the Pilot Area and compiling this information on a map. It was then intended to prepare the mining subsidence map from this map by back analysing subsidence incidents to determine the hazardous areas. This simple approach could not be followed for two reasons. First, the record of mining was incomplete and it was therefore necessary to define 'worked' seams and areas from the total historical record and not only from the surviving mine plans. Secondly, insufficient subsidence incidents were discovered in the Pilot Area to carry out meaningful back analysis. The study was extended to collect all readily available records of subsidence incidents throughout the Coalfield. A total of 388 were traced, mainly dating from 1960. About threequarters were collapses through superficial materials and were either close to the outcrop or above mine entries, the remaining 25% propagated to the ground surface through rock. The upper limit of migration was typically 8 times the extracted height where the dip was shallow, incrasing to as much as 18 times for steep dips. Selected grout contracts and opencast mining sites were also examined to gain information on the present condition of old workings and to study the 'reputations' of the various seams for voids. The results of the coalfield study were applied to the Pilot Area to produce a 1: 10 000 scale Development Advice Map, 'Mining Subsidence for use by developers and planners'. The map is zoned to show areas where specialist advice is necessary to support a planning application and it also shows all mine entries traced by the desk study. The method of production is general for the South Wales Coalfield and further maps could be prepared, using the Coalfield Study, quickly and cheaply.

entry.dc:title: Environmental planning and mineral development: The case of Hemerdon Mine
entry.dc:creator: Jones A.R.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geological Society Engineering Geology Special Publication
entry.dc:description: In 1981 a planning application was submitted to mine tungsten and tin at Hemerdon, near Plymouth, close to the edge of Dartmoor National Park. Considerable concern was expressed about the possible environmental damage which could result from this major opencast mining and waste disposal operation. Against this are set the potential benefits to the local and national economy. After a public inquiry in 1982 the Secretary of State refused permission but indicated improvements to the visual aspects of the processing plant and waste disposal area which would be regarded more favourably in a new submission. A revised plan was submitted in 1985 which, while still not satisfying objectors, was passed by Devon County Council, subject to conditions.

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST MINING - A SUCCESS STORY.
entry.dc:creator: Cotgrove P.
entry.dc:description: In the UK, opencast mining of all vested coal is carried out under the auspices of British Coal represented by the Opencast Executive in England and Wales and by Scottish Area north of the border. As in any manufacturing or extractive industry productivity is the cornerstone, and opencast mining is no exception. This review covers economics, plant capacity, manpower reductions, product quality and mining costs.

entry.dc:title: Reducing Risk of Accidents Thanks to the Improvement of Materials Handling in the Quarrying Industry.
entry.dc:creator: de la Rupelle G.
entry.dc:description: Quarrying and opencast mining inevitably involves the loading, transport, unloading and crushing of the excavated materials. Extraction of such materials is essential to satisfy the basic needs of a modern economy and is therefore inevitable. It must, however, be conducted in such a way as to minimize environmental nuisances such as noise, dust, vibration and disfigurement of the landscape and to ensure that the workforce enjoy the best possible safety standards and working conditions. Prevention has a major part to play, both in protecting the environment and avoiding accidents to the workforce within the site. Realistic preventive legislation tailored to the industry and taking account of the state of the art is necessary to provide mine and quarry operators with guidance in these important areas. In order to prevent nuisance and accidents, one must choose good loading, transport and crushing plant and maintain it in accordance with good working practices.

entry.dc:title: Typical mining methods proposed for working a large complex opencast mining block in the Jharia Coalfields
entry.dc:creator: Ghosh S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The Jharia Coalfield has one of the highest concentrations of seams containing the only metallurgical coal reserve in the country. The coalfield has been exploited by both opencast and underground methods of mining over many decades. The latter largely consisted of bord and pillar working in multi-section, multi-seam operations without much forethought of the subsequent liquidation of the coal pillars. With the demand of coking coal rising, the only practicable method of exploiting these pillars is to go for large-scale opencast mining. This calls for new as well as modified methods of opencast mining. This paper presents some typical mining methods proposed to exploit coal by opencast mining under these conditions.

entry.dc:title: Casting of overburden by directional blasting
entry.dc:creator: Ali S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The importance of opencast mining in Indian mining industry is examined. It is shown that casting of overburden by directional blasting can be used successfully to reduce costs in excavating and handling large volumes of overburden. The advantages and the factors affecting directional blasting are examined. The effects of air drag, size of fragments and initial velocity on casting factor are also examined. Ballistic tables and nomographs available for designing directional blasts are mentioned.

entry.dc:title: GROUND WATER CONTROL FOR OPENCAST MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Cashman P.M.
entry.dc:description: There are two broad elements to the control of groundwater at opencast mines, namely, the control of water ingress to the site and the collection and subsequent disposal of effluent from the site. In this paper, the author examines slope stability; site investigation, 'heave' and effluent control.

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST TECHNOLOGY.
entry.dc:creator: Couzens K.
entry.dc:description: Within British Coal today, opencast mining is the responsibility of the Opencast Executive and, in Scotland, of Scotland Area management. Opencast mining is a low-cost source of domestically produced energy for the British economy, most of the 14 million tonnes a year costing not more than POUND 1 a gigajoule to extract. Because opencast coal is often low in chlorine and ash content, it can be used for blending, which makes some otherwise unsaleable deep-mined coal acceptable to customers. Since the introduction of opencast mining operations in the UK some 460 million tonnes of coal have been produced which could not have been covered by traditional deep mining methods.

entry.dc:title: Investigation of Labour Conditions and the State of the Osteo-articular System in Excavator Machine Operators Engaged in Opencast Mining.
entry.dc:creator: Grigoryan E.
entry.dc:description: The working conditions of excavator operators and occupation related illnesses of osteo-articular system are analyzed. The hygienic evaluation of conditions in open pit mining under general vibrations and adverse microclimate is discussed. The result of X-ray examinations of spine and arms and changes in osteo-articular system are described.

entry.dc:title: SEALING WALLS IN OPENCAST MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Strzodka K.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: Lignite seams that do not immediately lie at surface level are mostly covered by interstratified coarse-grained or fine-grained layers. In most cases these layers are water-bearing and therefore must be drained before mining operations can begin. The article reports experience with sealing walls at the Ruedersdorf, Jaenschwalde and Berzdorf mines in the German Democratic Republic.

entry.dc:title: The influence of nitrogen and early drainage on production from grazed and cut grassland restored after opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: Baker A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
entry.dc:description: A review of past and present grassland management on land restored from opencast mining suggests that the most noticeable changes have been increased nitrogen fertiliser use and earlier installation of permanent under‐drainage. A programme of research is described which aimed to examine the effect of early drainage on perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne S23) grown for grazing, frequent cutting or silage production on sites previously opencast mined for coal, and to consider how these options affected both the short‐term productivity and the long‐term restoration of the soil. The results demonstrate that satisfactory herbage production is possible on restored land provided moderate levels of fertiliser are applied. Grass was utilised at high levels of intensity with no detrimental effects on sward or soil. Highest yields were obtained when grass was cut for silage, and under this regime early drainage led to a significant increase in herbage production each year of the study. When grazing was practised, drainage only led to increased total herbage production in wet years although benefits were seen in spring and in the overall sheep carrying capacity of the land. Clover inclusion in the cut swards only increased yield when less than 200 kg N ha<sup>−1</sup> year<sup>−1</sup> was applied. Copyright © 1987 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST TECHNOLOGY.
entry.dc:creator: Couzens K.
entry.dc:description: British Coal's opencast mining operations are in one sense a continuation of the oldest coal mining activities in Britain when, in mediaeval times and earlier, coal was dug from surface outcrops or seams near the surface.

entry.dc:title: GIANT EXTRACTION MACHINES FOR OPENCAST MINES: PART II.
entry.dc:creator: Wild J.
entry.dc:description: Without doubt some of the most spectacular stripping machines used in opencast mining operations in the world are those constructed by the Vitkovice Steel works situated in Czechoslovakia. A number of these machines are constructed in excavator or stacker form with walking undercarriages and linked by long-distance conveyors.

entry.dc:title: GEOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF OPENCAST MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Kelly D.
entry.dc:description: Prospecting policy and practice can be summed up under five headings: the finding of coal potential; the proving of coal reserves; presentation of the data upon which the decision to proceed can be made; production of contract documents which form the legal basis of the relationship between the National Coal Board and an appointed contractor; and provision of a back up service on operational sites. Each is discussed in more detail.

entry.dc:title: GIANT EXTRACTION MACHINES FOR OPENCAST MINES: PART I.
entry.dc:creator: Wild J.
entry.dc:description: Opencast mine operators are required to mine deep and to deal with great quantities of groundwater as a result of the steadily deteriorating overburden to coal ratio. Under the present conditions 69% more overburden had to be removed in 1980 than 20 years earlier. Hence larger and more efficient digging and dumping machines are developed and opencast mining techniques that will result in shorter hauling distances are applied. The equipment employed, such as bucket ladder and bucket wheel excavators plus dumping machines, like overburden conveyor bridges bridges and spreaders all of matching capacity, is described in the article.

entry.dc:title: PWH/PAURAT C-MINER: A NEW MACHINE FOR CONTINUOUS MINING OF HARD MATERIALS IN OPENCAST MINES.
entry.dc:creator: Sagner R.
entry.dc:description: Although the continuous-Miner of PHB Weserhuette AG and Paurat GmbH represents a new opencast mining technique, its subassemblies comprise components well proven in opencast and underground mining. The flexible concept of the continuous-Miner provides a broad scope for versatile opencast duty in conjunction with conveyor system and truck haulage. Combining three operations - 'cutting', 'crushing', 'loading' - the continuous mining machine can selectively remove thin seams of hard materials. Compared with conventional surface miners, its numerous advantages and low operating costs make this machine an economic and technical enrichment of the opencast sector.

entry.dc:title: LONG-TERM PLANNING FOR THE REHABILITATION OF OPENCAST WORKINGS.
entry.dc:creator: Wells J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy
entry.dc:description: An account is given of the planning required for the rehabilitation of land that is to be disturbed by opencast mining, and of the preparation of rehabilitation plans for submission to the Inspector of Mines. The plans include the provisions that are to be made to allow for climatic conditions, land use, vegetation and wildlife, surface-water resources, geology and ground water, soils, land capability, rehabilitation method, location of discard dumps and slurry ponds, pollution control, and costs. Monitoring of the operation is the only way that the rehabilitation plan can be improved, and both monitoring and planning are essential when provision is being made for the closure of a mine.

entry.dc:title: (Geology of coal deposits. 1. Fundamental problems).
entry.dc:creator: Petrescu I.
entry.dc:description: There are seven main chapters in the multi-authored book. 1) Chemical composition, physical and technical properties of coal. 2) Coal petrography, 3) Classifications of coals, 4) The main types of coals. 5) Origin of coal and coal deposits. 6) Special problems referring to the biostratigraphy of the main formation periods of coal deposits. 7) Principles of economic geology regarding the coal deposits: a) prospecting and exploration; b) coal reserve estimation; c) hydrogeology; d) underground and opencast mining; e) underground gasification. Both worldwide and Romanian aspects are covered.-M.A.Bass

entry.dc:title: A phytosociological study of a mid‐altitude heath in County Durham, Northern England
entry.dc:creator: Hughes J.
entry.dc:description: A phytosociological survey of Hedleyhope Fell, a mid‐Durham heath, was carried out. Much of the Fell is rank Nardus grassland, with damper Juncus and Eriophorum patches. Disturbed areas to the west are covered by poor Agrostis/Trifolium/Festuca grasslands. The eastern end of the Fell forms a locally valuable area of heathland. 115 relevés were taken and 131 species of plant recorded. Classification by two‐way indicator species analysis suggested the delimitation of 19 noda. The principal ordination axes, produced by detrended correspondence analysis, emphasised the importance of soil moisture gradients, organic/mineral soil gradients and levels of disturbance in determining the vegetation. The Fell, at 300 m, falls between the lowland heaths of southern England and the upland mires of the north. Indeed, its vegetation contains some assemblages and species characteristic of both habitats. The heaths of central, mid‐altitude County Durham are found where the coal measures lie close to the surface and so this habitat type has suffered extensively from opencast mining activity in the recent past. Proposed opencast sites, if they go ahead, will destroy the Fell. Copyright © 1986, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Geoveterinary aspects of Pb, Zn, Cu and Cd concentrations in part of the Pennines.
entry.dc:creator: Ineson P.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geology in the Real World the Kingsley Dunham Volume
entry.dc:description: High concentrations of Pb, Zn, Cu and Cd have been reported in streams, stream sediments, soils and herbage of the South Pennines. These anomalous metal values may be due to geochemical leakage haloes over veins, contamination from active industrial pollution, opencast mining operations, reworking of spoil heaps (mine tailings) or disused smelting sites. Aerial photographic interpretations, together with geological, geochemical and botanical surveys indicate potentially toxic areas known locally as 'belland ground'. The agricultural community and veterinary surgeons have long experience of the effects such ground has on crops and livestock management.-J.M.H.
